chapter: Hite tours, postwar L.A. and the Central Avenue scene
title: Hampton Sextet records: Bouncing at the Beacon, Open House
summary: The early Victor sides made between rehearsals, with Royal's tunes and Irving Ashby's.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: My first record date: sessions, personnel, discography

blocks.x: I guess so. It would give anybody an idea of what kind of band they might like to have. It must have been quite an experience. Nice to have been able to record that. Back to the book, it says here, playing alto and clarinet, that you were first of all in the Hampton Sextet, a group which included pianist Sir Charles Thompson (PHONETIC) and saxist-violinist Ray Perry (PHONETIC) and that you recorded with that unit for Victor, playing notably artistic solos on "Bouncing at the Beacon (PHONETIC)," and other sides." Is that right?
"And then, Hampton enlarged his group to the forces of a big band. That is, you enlarged it, (inaudible) to the proportions of a big band.

Well, it was already a big band when we made those things. In between the rehearsals, Lionel wanted to make some records and we just did that. Those fellas had just met each other, the fellas that you afore mentioned had just met each other probably a week or so before and so we made up some tunes and recorded them. I think "Bouncing at the Beacon" was mine, was my tune, and another tune called -- we named after a guy that had a radio program up in San Francisco called "Open

House," "The Open House Show." That was my tune called "Open House." Then there was another tune that Irving Ashby, (PHONETIC) the guitar player, wrote called "Stratosphere." No, it was not "Stratosphere," "Altitude," and some other things like that.
